title: All's Well That Ends Well
author: William Shakespeare
setting: The Countess's house at Rossillon, the King of France's court in Paris, and the city and camp of Florence during a war with Siena
lengthNote: Around 3,000 lines across twenty-three scenes, with Parolles, the Clown and the soldiers' camp speaking largely in prose
openingLine: In delivering my son from me, I bury a second husband.
summary: Helena, the orphaned daughter of a famous physician, has been brought up in the Countess of Rossillon's household and is in love with the Countess's son Bertram, who is far above her in rank. She cures the dying King of France with one of her father's remedies and is allowed to choose a husband from the lords at court. She chooses Bertram, who is ordered into the marriage and leaves for the war in Florence that night, writing that she may call him husband only when she has the ring off his finger and a child of his to show. Helena follows him, finds the young woman he is trying to seduce, and takes her place in his bed. Beside this runs the unmasking of Bertram's companion Parolles, a braggart whom his fellow officers blindfold and frighten into betraying everyone he knows.

sourceText.label: Project Gutenberg text of the Complete Works of William Shakespeare (eBook 100)
sourceText.note: Every quotation here is taken word for word from this text, which spells the Countess's county Rossillon. Act, scene and line references follow the traditional Globe numbering, from which modern editions vary by a few lines, most of all in the prose scenes.

atAGlance.label: Written
atAGlance.note: No record fixes the date. Editors have proposed years from about 1602 to 1606, most often placing it close to Measure for Measure.

atAGlance.label: First printed
atAGlance.note: No quarto is known. The First Folio prints it among the comedies, and every modern edition depends on that one text.

atAGlance.label: Source
atAGlance.note: The story of Giletta of Narbonne from the Decameron, which reached English readers in William Painter's Palace of Pleasure. Parolles and the Countess have no counterpart there.

atAGlance.label: Shape
atAGlance.note: The action moves from Rossillon to Paris, back to Rossillon, out to Florence and its camp, and home by way of Marseilles.

structure.label: Act I
structure.title: A ward in love above her station
structure.summary: The Countess's household is in mourning, and her son Bertram leaves for Paris to become the King's ward. Helena, left behind, admits to herself that she loves him and that he is as far above her as a star. At court the King is dying of a fistula his doctors have given up on. Back at Rossillon the Countess learns of Helena's love from her steward, draws a confession out of her, and gives her leave to take her dead father's remedy to Paris.

scenes.title: Mourning at Rossillon
scenes.summary: The Countess blesses Bertram before he leaves. Alone, Helena says she has forgotten her father's face and remembers only Bertram's, trades jokes about virginity with Parolles, and ends the scene resolved to act.

scenes.title: A sick king
scenes.summary: The King lets his young lords serve on either side of the war between Florence and Siena, praises Bertram’s dead father at length, and asks how long it is since the famous physician of Rossillon died.

scenes.title: The Countess and Helena
scenes.summary: The Clown asks leave to marry Isbel. The Steward reports that he overheard Helena confessing her love to herself, and the Countess tests her with the word mother until she kneels and admits it.

structure.label: Act II
structure.title: The cure and the choosing
structure.summary: Helena persuades the King to try her remedy, staking her life on curing him within two days, and asks as her fee a husband of her choosing. The cure works. She passes along a line of young lords, chooses Bertram, and is refused in front of the court because she is a poor physician's daughter. The King overrules him and has the marriage performed that night. Bertram decides on the spot to go to the Tuscan wars, sends Helena home to his mother with a message, and rides away before the marriage is consummated.

scenes.title: Doctor she
scenes.summary: Bertram is kept at court as too young for the war. Lafew brings in Helena, who wears down the King's refusal in rhymed couplets and names her price.

scenes.title: O Lord, sir
scenes.summary: The Clown shows the Countess his answer that fits every question at court, and is sent to Paris with a letter for Helena.

scenes.title: The choice
scenes.summary: Lafew and Parolles marvel at the cure. Helena chooses Bertram, the King lectures him on virtue and title and then threatens him into consent, and Lafew picks a quarrel with Parolles that exposes him as all scarves and no substance.

scenes.title: Sent home
scenes.summary: Parolles tells Helena that Bertram must put off his marriage rights. Lafew warns Bertram about Parolles, and Bertram sends Helena away with a letter for his mother, refusing her a parting kiss.

structure.label: Act III
structure.title: Letters, flight and a pilgrim in Florence
structure.summary: Bertram's letters reach Rossillon. One tells his mother he has wedded Helena without bedding her; the other sets Helena his two impossible conditions. The Countess disowns her son, and Helena leaves the house at night, writing that she has gone as a barefoot pilgrim to Saint Jaques. Bertram is made general of the Duke of Florence's horse. Helena turns up in Florence, lodges with a widow whose daughter Diana is being pursued by Bertram, tells the widow who she is, and pays her to help with a plan to put herself in Diana's place.

scenes.title: The Duke of Florence
scenes.summary: The Duke complains that the French king will not send help, and is told that young Frenchmen will come of their own accord.

scenes.title: Two letters
scenes.summary: The Countess reads that her son has run away. Helena reads his conditions aloud, and alone she blames herself for sending him into the line of musket fire.

scenes.title: General of the horse, and Saint Jaques' pilgrim
scenes.summary: The Duke gives Bertram his command. At Rossillon the Steward reads Helena's sonnet-letter, and the Countess orders him to write to Bertram that his wife has gone.

scenes.title: The troops go by
scenes.summary: The Widow, Diana and Mariana watch the soldiers pass. A pilgrim who says she is bound for Saint Jaques hears Diana describe the French count who is courting her, and the man who carries his messages.

scenes.title: Two plots laid
scenes.summary: The French lords persuade Bertram to let Parolles try to recover the lost drum so that they can ambush him. Helena gives the Widow gold and sets out the terms for the night to come.

structure.label: Act IV
structure.title: Parolles captured, and the bed-trick
structure.summary: Parolles, out alone at night inventing wounds to explain his failure, is seized by his own side speaking nonsense and believes he has been taken by the enemy. Bertram gives Diana his ancestral ring and agrees to a silent hour in her dark chamber. The lords hear that a peace has been concluded and that Helena has died at the shrine. Later that night Parolles, still blindfolded, sells every secret he can think of while Bertram listens. Helena sets out for the King, and at Rossillon Lafew arranges for Bertram to marry his daughter.

scenes.title: The ambush
scenes.summary: Parolles talks himself through the lies he will need, is blindfolded by soldiers speaking gibberish, and offers to reveal the whole Florentine camp to save his life.

scenes.title: The ring
scenes.summary: Diana argues Bertram out of his family ring by using his own words about honour, and tells him to come to her window at midnight and not to speak.

scenes.title: The interrogation
scenes.summary: The lords discuss Bertram's seduction and the report of Helena's death. Parolles, questioned from a note, lies about troop numbers, slanders both Dumaine brothers and Bertram, and is shown who has been listening.

scenes.title: The fine's the crown
scenes.summary: Helena tells the Widow and Diana that she is believed dead and that they must go to the King, who she hears is at Marseilles.

scenes.title: A patch of velvet
scenes.summary: Lafew and the Countess mourn Helena and agree a match with Lafew's daughter. The Clown announces Bertram's return with a patch of velvet on his face.

structure.label: Act V
structure.title: The ring, and Helena’s return
structure.summary: Helena misses the King at Marseilles and follows him to Rossillon. Parolles, ragged and smelling of misfortune, is taken in by Lafew. The King forgives Bertram and approves the new match until he sees the ring Bertram offers as a token for Lafew's daughter: it is the one the King once gave Helena. Bertram lies about it, Diana arrives with a petition claiming him as her husband, and he lies about her too. Diana answers every question with a riddle until Helena enters, pregnant, with the ring and the letter that set the conditions.

scenes.title: Marseilles
scenes.summary: The King has already left. Helena gives her petition to a gentleman of the court, who is going to Rossillon.

scenes.title: Fortune's cat
scenes.summary: The Clown holds his nose at Parolles. Lafew gives him a coin, asks after his drum and promises he shall eat.

scenes.title: The reckoning at Rossillon
scenes.summary: The ring, Bertram's arrest, Diana's petition, Parolles as a witness, the riddle of one that's dead is quick, and Helena's entrance.

scenes.title: The king's a beggar
scenes.summary: The actor who has played the King steps out of the play to ask the audience for applause, in the same rhymed couplets the play has used for its bargains.

characters.name: Helena
characters.role: Daughter of the physician Gerard de Narbon, brought up by the Countess
characters.summary: She drives every turn of the plot, and she keeps describing herself as low, poor and unworthy while she does it. She stakes her life on a cure the King's doctors have abandoned, chooses her husband in front of the court, obeys his order to go home, and then slips away from it by night. The bed trick is her design, paid for with her own gold. She speaks the play's title twice, each time as a way of carrying on.
characters.clue: She takes a dead man's prescription to a dying king and asks to be paid in a husband.

characters.name: Bertram
characters.role: Count of Rossillon, the Countess's son
characters.summary: He is young, newly fatherless and a ward of the King, and he wants to be at the war. Ordered to marry a woman he calls a poor physician's daughter, he gives in to a threat, leaves on the wedding night and wins honour as a cavalry commander in Florence. He courts Diana with music and oaths, hands over the ring of his house to get her into bed, and at court tells lie after lie about the ring and about her. His last lines promise love on a condition.
characters.clue: He tells his wife she may call him husband when she has his ring and his child, and gives both away himself in the dark.

characters.name: The Countess of Rossillon
characters.summary: She opens the play in black for her husband and ends it asking the King to forgive her son. Her first response to Helena's love is alarm, God shield you mean it not, and within a hundred lines she is giving her means and attendants for the trip to Paris. On reading Bertram's letter she takes Helena's side against him without hesitation, and in the last scene she identifies the ring Diana holds as the heirloom of her house.
characters.clue: She tells a ward she is a mother to her and watches the girl go white at the word.

characters.name: The King of France
characters.role: Ruler of the court at Paris, dying when the play begins
characters.summary: He has given up hope of a cure and at first will not let an unknown young woman try, then agrees on condition that she dies if she fails. Cured, he keeps his promise by force, making a fine speech on virtue against title and following it with threats when Bertram is unpersuaded. In the last scene he forgives Bertram, suspects him of murder, arrests him, loses patience with Diana's riddles, and at the end offers Diana a husband of her choosing and a dowry, repeating the bargain that started the trouble.
characters.clue: He pays for his cure with somebody else's son.

characters.name: Parolles
characters.summary: His name is French for words, and he is mostly made of them. Helena knows him for a liar and a coward in the first scene, and Lafew sees through his scarves at their first meeting. He urges Bertram to the war, swears he will recover a lost drum, and when his own comrades take him blindfold he betrays the army and slanders everyone in it. Stripped of his captaincy, he decides to live as the thing he is, and the man who first exposed him ends up feeding him.
characters.clue: He promises to bring back a lost drum, and is himself brought in blindfold instead.

relationships.label: exposed by, and at last taken in by

characters.name: Lafew
characters.role: An old lord of the French court
characters.summary: He is the play's plain judge of character. He brings Helena to the King with a joke about being Cressida's uncle, marvels at the cure, and is the first to see that Parolles is a window of lattice he can look straight through. After Helena's supposed death he proposes his own daughter for Bertram, withdraws the offer as soon as Diana's petition is read, and ends the play in tears, borrowing Parolles's handkerchief and telling him to wait on him at home.
characters.clue: He calls a man a window of lattice, and at the end his eyes smell onions.

relationships.label: offers his daughter to, then withdraws

characters.name: Diana
characters.role: Daughter of a widow of Florence, courted by Bertram
characters.summary: In her first scene Mariana warns her against the French count and his go-between, and she never wavers. In her one scene alone with Bertram she takes his oaths apart and gets his ring by turning his own argument about honour against him. At court she plays the witness who will not give a straight answer, claims to be married and a maid in the same breath, and risks prison to hold the truth back until Helena comes in.
characters.clue: She makes a midnight appointment with a count and arranges not to keep it.

relationships.label: stands in for, and is stood in for by
petitions, and is offered a husband by

characters.name: The Widow of Florence
characters.summary: She says she was well born and has come down in the world, and she hesitates to put her reputation at risk. Helena's proofs of rank and a purse of gold persuade her, and Diana later says her mother told her exactly how Bertram would woo. She travels with Helena to Marseilles and Rossillon and stands beside Diana in front of the King.
characters.clue: She is promised three thousand crowns towards her daughter's marriage for one night's arrangements.

characters.name: The Clown (Lavache)
characters.summary: He wants to marry Isbel because the flesh drives him, loses interest after a trip to court, and entertains the Countess with an answer for every question at court. His jokes about cuckolds, the devil and the broad gate to the great fire run close to the play's darker matter. Parolles alone gives his name, Lavache, when he comes begging in the last act and the Clown will not stand downwind of him.
characters.clue: He has one answer that fits every question at court, and the answer is O Lord, sir.

characters.name: The two French lords (the Dumaine brothers)
characters.role: Brothers serving with Bertram in the Florentine war
characters.summary: They leave the court for the war in 2.1, carry letters between Florence and Rossillon, and set the trap for Parolles because they know him better than Bertram does. One leads the ambush in a language of his own invention. Waiting for Bertram in 4.3 they judge his seduction of Diana with a frankness nobody uses to his face, and one of them sums the whole play up in a sentence about a mingled yarn.
characters.clue: Asked about the Dumaine brothers, Parolles slanders both of them while both stand in the room.

themes.name: Birth and merit
themes.summary: Bertram refuses Helena for one reason, her father's profession, and the King answers that honour comes from deeds and that he can supply the title himself. The play sets a count who inherited everything beside a physician's daughter who earned her place at court.
themes.development: The argument is won in words in 2.3 and settled by force, and Bertram’s conduct in Florence shows whether his birth has made him fit for the rank he defends.

themes.name: Forced marriage
themes.summary: The central marriage is ordered by a king, performed within hours and abandoned the same night. For the rest of the play Helena works to make a legal bond into a real marriage, on the terms her husband wrote to be impossible.
themes.development: The last scene is a second wedding in all but form, and it closes on Bertram's conditional promise and the King's offer to arrange another marriage for Diana.

themes.name: Honour
themes.summary: Bertram's ring is the honour of his house, Diana's chastity is hers, Parolles's lost drum is an instrument of honour, and the King says honour grows from acts. Each version is tested and several are traded away.
themes.development: Bertram wins honour in the field and loses it in bed and at court, and the First Lord's mingled yarn describes the mix.

themes.name: Words, clothes and courage
themes.summary: Parolles lives by scarves, garters and big talk, and Lafew says the soul of the man is his clothes. His exposure in 4.3 strips off each layer until only a frightened man who wants to eat is left.
themes.development: Bertram trusts the performance and learns what it covers only when he hears himself described by it, and he goes on performing at court in the last act.

themes.name: Conditions, tokens and proof
themes.summary: Bertram's refusal takes the form of two conditions, the ring and the child, and the plot is Helena's way of satisfying them. Rings, letters and a pregnancy carry the final scene, where the King can only believe what he is shown.
themes.development: Two rings cross in the dark in Florence and have to be traced back to their owners in front of the court, while Diana's riddles keep the proof back until Helena can deliver it.

themes.name: Inheritance
themes.summary: Helena inherits her father's skill and a paper of prescriptions, Bertram inherits his father's face, title and ring. The Countess prays that Bertram will succeed his father in manners as well as shape, and the King looks for the father's moral parts in the son.
themes.development: The inherited remedy makes Helena’s fortune, the inherited ring catches Bertram out, and the play ends with an heir already on the way.

themes.name: Pursuit in love
themes.summary: Helena chooses and pursues, which reverses the usual pattern of comedy, and Bertram flees her while pursuing another woman. The play makes both kinds of wanting uncomfortable to watch.
themes.development: Helena says in 4.4 that men can make sweet use of what they hate. The bed trick joins his lust and her love in one act that neither of them sees in the same way.

techniques.name: The bed trick
techniques.definition: A plot device in which one person secretly takes another's place in a sexual encounter, usually in the dark, to bind or expose the partner.
techniques.inThisBook: Helena takes Diana's place in Bertram's bed on a night he has been told to keep silent and leave within the hour. The device comes from Boccaccio, and the play keeps it offstage, so the audience hears of it only through Helena’s plans and Diana’s riddles.

techniques.name: Stage property
techniques.definition: An object handled on stage that carries far more weight than its use in the scene explains.
techniques.inThisBook: Two rings drive the plot: Bertram's ancestral ring, which Diana gets from him, and the King's ring, which Helena puts on Bertram's finger in the dark. The last scene is spent working out who gave which ring to whom.

techniques.name: Letters
techniques.definition: Written messages read aloud or reported on stage, which carry action and information across distances the characters cannot cross.
techniques.inThisBook: Bertram's two letters in 3.2 set the plot's terms, Helena's pilgrim sonnet in 3.4 covers her escape, Parolles's letter to Diana convicts him in 4.3, and Diana's petition in 5.3 brings Bertram's lies to a stop.

techniques.name: The gulling scene
techniques.definition: A comic episode in which a group plays an elaborate trick on a vain or foolish character to expose him.
techniques.inThisBook: The drum plot of 4.1 and 4.3 captures Parolles with nonsense words and a blindfold, and the questioning is conducted with Bertram present, so the victim's betrayals land on the man he is betraying.

techniques.name: Rhymed couplets
techniques.definition: Pairs of rhyming lines, which give speech the finality of a proverb or the formality of a contract.
techniques.inThisBook: The play shifts into rhyme at its moments of decision and bargaining: Helena's resolve at the end of 1.1, her bargain with the King in 2.1, the King's speech on honour in 2.3, and Bertram's last promise. The Epilogue is in the same form.

techniques.name: Soliloquy
techniques.definition: A speech delivered by a character alone on stage, giving the audience direct access to thoughts hidden from others.
techniques.inThisBook: Helena has two in 1.1, which take her from hopeless adoration to a plan, and a third in 3.2, where she decides to leave France so that Bertram can come home. Parolles's short soliloquy after his exposure is the most honest thing he says.

techniques.name: Prose against verse
techniques.definition: The switch between prose and verse within a play, used to mark changes of class, mood or seriousness.
techniques.inThisBook: Parolles, the Clown, Lafew in his quarrels and the soldiers of the camp speak prose, while the court and Helena speak verse. The lords' sober judgement of Bertram in 4.3 comes in prose, which strips it of ceremony.

quotations.text: Love all, trust a few, Do wrong to none.
quotations.speaker: Countess
quotations.context: Blessing Bertram as he leaves Rossillon to become the King's ward in Paris.
quotations.analysis: Nine words of a mother's advice, and the rest of the play shows her son getting every clause wrong. He trusts Parolles, the one companion everyone warns him about, and before the end he has wronged his wife and lied to the King. The same speech hopes his goodness will share with his birthright, which is exactly what Bertram fails to manage.

quotations.text: 'Twere all one That I should love a bright particular star, And think to wed it, he is so above me.
quotations.speaker: Helena
quotations.context: Alone after Bertram has left for Paris, admitting that her tears are for him and not for her father.
quotations.analysis: Helena measures the social distance between them in astronomy. Bertram is a star, she may be comforted only by his collateral light, and marrying him would be as absurd as wedding a star. The image gives his rank the fixed order of the heavens, and by the end of the same scene she will argue that the sky leaves people free to act.

quotations.text: Virginity, by being once lost, may be ten times found; by being ever kept, it is ever lost.
quotations.speaker: Parolles
quotations.context: Bantering with Helena, who has asked how a virgin might defend herself against men.
quotations.analysis: Parolles talks about virginity the way a merchant talks about hoarding: goods kept lose value and goods spent multiply. The paradox is glib, and the play then carries it out in earnest, since Helena's virginity is given up in a dark room in Florence and comes back as a child and a husband. His prose joke turns into her method.

quotations.text: Our remedies oft in ourselves do lie, Which we ascribe to heaven: the fated sky Gives us free scope
quotations.speaker: Helena
quotations.context: Alone again after Parolles leaves, closing the first scene.
quotations.analysis: Earlier in the scene the star was out of reach; here it becomes a fated sky that gives her free scope, and the verse turns to rhyming couplets as her mind is made up. Her last words in the scene name the plan before anyone else knows it: the king's disease. From this point the plot runs on what she decides to do.

quotations.text: He that of greatest works is finisher Oft does them by the weakest minister.
quotations.speaker: Helena
quotations.context: Refusing to accept the King's dismissal after he tells her his learned doctors have given him up.
quotations.analysis: A proverb about Providence is Helena’s answer to the whole college of physicians, and her lack of standing becomes the evidence for her claim. A young woman carrying a dead father's prescription becomes, in this couplet, the kind of instrument heaven prefers. The King had just refused to prostitute his malady to empirics, and within fifty lines he agrees to try her.

quotations.text: A poor physician's daughter my wife! Disdain Rather corrupt me ever!
quotations.speaker: Bertram
quotations.context: Told by the King, in front of the assembled lords, that Helena has chosen him.
quotations.analysis: His objection is purely one of rank, and he makes it in front of the man she has just cured. Poor and physician's are the insults; he says nothing against her looks or her honesty. He would rather be corrupted by disdain for ever than accept her, and the line hands the King the argument he answers for the next thirty lines.

quotations.text: From lowest place when virtuous things proceed, The place is dignified by the doer's deed.
quotations.speaker: King
quotations.analysis: Worth lies in what people do and titles are only words, the King argues, and he puts it in rhymed couplets that give it the finish of a proverb. When Bertram is still unpersuaded, the King drops the argument and threatens to throw him into the staggers. Merit is defended in principle and enforced by royal command, which leaves the audience unsure which of the two has won.

quotations.text: War is no strife To the dark house and the detested wife.
quotations.speaker: Bertram
quotations.context: Moments after the wedding, telling Parolles that he will go to the Tuscan wars and send Helena home.
quotations.analysis: The couplet weighs a marriage against a battlefield and finds the battlefield easier. A dark house suggests both mourning and confinement, and the line makes Helena a place to escape from. In 2.1 Bertram was kept from the war as too young; now the marriage gives him his excuse to go.

quotations.text: there can be no kernal in this light nut; the soul of this man is his clothes
quotations.speaker: Lafew
quotations.context: Warning Bertram about Parolles on the day of his departure.
quotations.analysis: Lafew has spent two scenes mocking Parolles's scarves and garters, and here he reduces the man to an empty shell and a wardrobe. The drum plot proves him right in 4.3, when the blindfold comes off and nothing is left under the costume. Bertram hears the warning and ignores it, which tells the audience as much about his judgement as about Parolles.

quotations.text: When thou canst get the ring upon my finger, which never shall come off, and show me a child begotten of thy body that I am father to, then call me husband
quotations.speaker: Bertram (in a letter read by Helena)
quotations.context: Helena reads Bertram's letter aloud at Rossillon, in front of his mother and the two lords who carried it.
quotations.analysis: Bertram writes his refusal as a pair of conditions he believes impossible, and signs it off with a pun, in such a then I write a never. Without meaning to he has drafted a contract. Helena reads it as one and meets each clause to the letter, which is how his refusal becomes the plan for the rest of the plot.

quotations.text: He was my son, But I do wash his name out of my blood, And thou art all my child.
quotations.speaker: Countess
quotations.context: Comforting Helena after both of them have read Bertram's letters.
quotations.analysis: Disowning her son in favour of her ward, the Countess completes the adoption she offered in 1.3. Wash and blood treat kinship as a stain that can be cleaned away, a startling claim from the character who cares most about family in the play. The past tense of He was my son does the disowning before the rest of the sentence explains it.

quotations.text: Is wicked meaning in a lawful deed, And lawful meaning in a lawful act, Where both not sin, and yet a sinful fact.
quotations.speaker: Helena
quotations.context: Closing the scene in which she pays the Widow and plans to take Diana's place in Bertram's bed that night.
quotations.analysis: In a riddle, Helena works through the ethics of the bed trick. Bertram intends adultery and will in fact sleep with his wife; she intends something lawful and still takes part in a deception. The balanced clauses keep both sides in view without settling the question, and the last phrase, a sinful fact, concedes that something about the deed remains wrong.

quotations.text: Mine honour's such a ring; My chastity's the jewel of our house, Bequeathed down from many ancestors
quotations.speaker: Diana
quotations.context: Bertram has just refused to give up his ring, calling it an honour of his house bequeathed down from many ancestors.
quotations.analysis: Diana repeats Bertram's own sentence back to him with one noun changed, so that his reason for keeping the ring becomes her reason for keeping her chastity. He has no answer that does not give way, and six lines later he hands the ring over. The exchange states the bargain the plot depends on: a man's heirloom against a woman's body, and both of them called honour.

quotations.text: The web of our life is of a mingled yarn, good and ill together
quotations.speaker: First Lord
quotations.context: The two French lords, waiting for Bertram in the camp, have been discussing his seduction of Diana and the news of Helena's death.
quotations.analysis: Plain prose from a minor character at the edge of the plot gives the play's summary of itself. Bertram has won honour in battle and disgrace at home in the same weeks, and the image of one cloth woven from two threads declines to sort him into good or bad. The sentence goes on to say that our virtues would be proud if our faults did not whip them, a fair description of the scene about to follow.

quotations.text: Simply the thing I am Shall make me live.
quotations.speaker: Parolles
quotations.context: Alone, after the blindfold is removed and his captors have each taken leave of him in mockery.
quotations.analysis: Exposed as a coward, a liar and a traitor, Parolles neither apologises nor collapses. He gives up the title of captain and resolves to eat, drink and sleep as the thing he is. The line is comic and oddly dignified, and it gives the plain account of himself that Bertram never gives, even in the last scene.

quotations.text: All's well that ends well; still the fine's the crown. Whate'er the course, the end is the renown.
quotations.speaker: Helena
quotations.context: Setting out with the Widow and Diana to find the King, who she has heard is at Marseilles.
quotations.analysis: Here the play’s title arrives as a proverb, and Helena explains it straight away. Fine means the end, and the end is what earns the crown, so an action is judged by how it turns out. It is a defence of her own methods, spoken just after the bed trick, and she repeats the proverb in 5.1 when the King has moved on and her plan looks as if it may fail.

quotations.text: 'Tis but the shadow of a wife you see, The name, and not the thing.
quotations.speaker: Helena
quotations.context: Entering at the end of Diana’s riddle, when the King wonders whether what he sees is real.
quotations.analysis: Calling herself a shadow, as if she were a ghost, Helena then puts the whole history of her marriage in six words: she has been Bertram's wife in title only. His answer, Both, both, grants her the thing as well as the name. How much he means by it the text leaves to the actor, since it gives him two words and no stage direction.

quotations.text: If she, my liege, can make me know this clearly, I'll love her dearly, ever, ever dearly.
quotations.speaker: Bertram
quotations.context: Bertram's last words in the play, after Helena has shown the ring and read back his letter.
quotations.analysis: His promise begins with If. He addresses the King and speaks of Helena in the third person, as though the marriage were still a case awaiting proof. The chime of clearly and dearly makes the couplet sound settled, and the repeated ever sounds eager, yet the condition stands, and Helena immediately offers ‘deadly divorce’ if her proof fails.

timeline.label: Boccaccio finishes the Decameron
timeline.detail: The ninth tale of the third day tells of Giletta of Narbonne, a physician's daughter who cures the King of France, is given Beltramo of Roussillon as her husband, and wins him back by meeting his conditions.

timeline.label: Painter's Palace of Pleasure
timeline.detail: William Painter's collection of translated tales puts the Giletta story into English, the most likely route by which it reached Shakespeare.

timeline.label: Meres lists a Love's Labour's Won
timeline.detail: Francis Meres names it among Shakespeare's comedies in Palladis Tamia. No play of that title survives. All's Well has been proposed as a candidate, with no evidence either way.

timeline.label: Measure for Measure played at court
timeline.detail: The other comedy of these years that depends on a bed trick was performed at Whitehall on 26 December. Most editors date All's Well near it.

timeline.label: Printed in the First Folio
timeline.detail: The only early text. It appears among the comedies, and no earlier quarto is known.

timeline.label: First recorded performance
timeline.detail: The play's securely recorded stage history begins at Goodman's Fields, more than a century after the Folio.

timeline.label: Johnson cannot like Bertram
timeline.detail: In his edition of Shakespeare, Samuel Johnson set out Bertram's offences and objected that the play dismisses him to happiness regardless.

timeline.label: Boas names the problem plays
timeline.detail: Frederick Boas grouped All's Well with Measure for Measure, Troilus and Cressida and Hamlet as plays that raise questions they do not resolve. The label has stuck to the comedies.

timeline.label: Guthrie at Stratford
timeline.detail: Tyrone Guthrie's Shakespeare Memorial Theatre production, designed by Tanya Moiseiwitsch, had Edith Evans as the Countess.

timeline.label: John Barton's RSC production
timeline.detail: Ian Richardson played Bertram, Lynn Farleigh Helena and Helen Mirren Diana. A television version followed in 1968.

timeline.label: BBC Television Shakespeare
timeline.detail: Elijah Moshinsky directed Angela Down as Helena, Ian Charleson as Bertram and Celia Johnson as the Countess. In the same year Trevor Nunn's RSC production cast Peggy Ashcroft as the Countess.

timeline.label: Marianne Elliott at the National Theatre
timeline.detail: Michelle Terry played Helena and Conleth Hill Parolles, in a production recorded for broadcast and often discussed for its handling of the ending.

places.name: Rossillon (Roussillon)
places.note: The Countess's house, where the play opens and ends. The historical county of Roussillon lay around Perpignan, on the Mediterranean side of the Pyrenees.

places.name: Paris
places.note: The King's court, where Helena cures him and chooses her husband in Act II.

places.name: Florence
places.note: The Duke's city and camp, where Bertram commands the horse, Parolles loses his drum, and the Widow lodges pilgrims.

places.name: Siena
places.note: Home of the Senoys, Florence's enemy in the war the young French lords go to join.

places.name: Marseilles
places.note: Where Helena expects to find the King in 4.4, and where she learns in 5.1 that he has already gone.

places.name: Santiago de Compostela
places.note: The shrine of Saint Jaques le Grand, to which Helena writes that she has gone barefoot. She is next seen in Florence.

criticalViews.summary: Samuel Johnson could not bring himself to like Bertram, who marries under threat, abandons his wife, lies when accused and is still sent off to happiness at the end. On this reading the comedy rewards a man who has done nothing to earn his reward, and the title reads as an evasion.
criticalViews.counter: The play seems aware of the objection. Bertram's last lines are conditional, the King's closing couplet says only that all yet seems well, and the Epilogue hands the verdict to the audience. The discomfort Johnson felt is written into the ending.

criticalViews.summary: Since Frederick Boas grouped it with Measure for Measure and Troilus and Cressida in 1896, the play has been read as a comedy in form that raises questions of rank, sex and consent it cannot settle. Its ending supplies the marriage and withholds the feeling.
criticalViews.counter: The label can flatten the play. Much of it is straightforward comedy, including the Clown and the whole drum plot, and the story of the clever wife who meets impossible conditions was an old and popular one that audiences would have recognised as a romance.

criticalViews.position: A folk tale taken at its word
criticalViews.summary: W. W. Lawrence argued in 1931 that the healing of a king and the fulfilment of impossible tasks are folk-tale motifs, and that an audience of the time would admire Helena as the heroine who carries them out. Judging her by modern ideas of courtship misreads the convention.
criticalViews.counter: Shakespeare adds exactly what the tale leaves out. Bertram is given a voice to say no with, the King’s force is shown on stage, and the bed trick puts Bertram in bed with a woman he did not choose. The changes pull against the convention, which is why modern productions return to questions of consent.

essayQuestions.question: Is Helena the heroine of a love story or the author of a trap?
plan: Start with the soliloquies in 1.1: the hopeless star speech, and then the couplets in which it becomes a plan.
Examine the bargain with the King in 2.1, where she stakes her life and asks for a husband as her fee, and the choosing scene in 2.3, where she offers to withdraw.
Read her letter from Saint Jaques in 3.4 against her arrival in Florence in 3.5, and decide what the pilgrimage was for.
Weigh the bed trick through her own words in 3.7 and 4.4, including the admission of a sinful fact and her line on men who make sweet use of what they hate.
Close on 5.3, where she offers deadly divorce if her proof fails, and judge whether the ending is her victory or her compromise.

essayQuestions.question: What does All's Well That Ends Well mean by honour?
plan: Set out the King's argument in 2.3 that honour comes from deeds and not from birth, and note that he enforces it with threats.
Compare the two rings in 4.2: Bertram's ring as the honour of his house and Diana's chastity as the jewel of hers.
Use Parolles's drum as the parody version, an instrument of honour that nobody needs until it is lost.
Look at Bertram's military reputation in Florence against his conduct in the same weeks, using the First Lord's mingled yarn.
Decide whose idea of honour the last scene rewards, and whose it simply ignores.

essayQuestions.question: How does the exposure of Parolles shape our judgement of Bertram?
essayQuestions.focus: The drum plot as a mirror of the main plot
plan: Begin with the warnings: Helena's soliloquy in 1.1, Lafew's attacks in 2.3 and 2.5, and Bertram's refusal to listen.
Show how the lords design the ambush in 3.6 so that Bertram will be present at the questioning.
Analyse 4.3, where Parolles betrays the army and describes Bertram to his face, and Bertram calls him a cat.
Set Parolles's soliloquy, simply the thing I am, beside Bertram's lies about the ring and about Diana in 5.3.
Conclude on who is punished, who is forgiven, and whether the two plots reach the same verdict.

discussionQuestions: The King forces Bertram to marry Helena and then argues that honour comes from deeds. Does the play agree with his argument, his method, or neither?
Helena twice speaks the title as a proverb. Is the play's ending well, and on whose terms?
Diana risks prison and her reputation in the last scene for a plan that is not hers. What does she gain from it?
Parolles is exposed, humiliated and then fed by the man who first saw through him. Why does the play let him off so lightly?
The Countess disowns her son and calls Helena all her child. How does her view of the marriage differ from the King's?
The bed trick happens offstage and is never shown. What difference would it make if it were?

related.why: Written in the same years, and also resolved by a bed trick in which a woman takes another's place in the dark to hold a man to a promise.
Another comedy whose last act turns on a ring a husband has given away, and on the wife who knows exactly where it went.
Falstaff's cowardice is exposed by a prank set up by his own companions, the model for the drum plot that unmasks Parolles.
Grouped with All's Well as a problem play, and just as unsentimental about honour, war and what a reputation is worth.
A later play in which a ring and a night in a bedroom decide a marriage, and a husband who has wronged his wife is forgiven in one crowded final scene.
